## Clarity, Quality, Novelty And Reproducibility:
> The explanation of the main approach in Sec. 3.3 is vague and I has difficulty understanding how the optimization problems (6) and (7) are solved. Besides, further details on how the authors design timelines and tasks in the experiments are not discussed. In general, the experiments are not reproducible based on the current writeup.

A: 

- *How the optimization problems (6) and (7) are solved?*:
    - *Relations of Problems (6) and (7)*: We define to find the optimal weights $\mathbf{w}^*$ and the final update gradient is obtained by $\mathbf{d}^*=\sum\_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbf{w}\_i\mathbf{g}\_i$ (Eq. (6)). To avoid the self-interference problem, we use a matrix $\mathbf{W}$ instead of the weight vector $w$, and solve with the proposed MaxDO approach (Eq. (7)).
    - *Solving Problem (7)*: The weight matrix $W$ contains two parts, the diagonal vector $\grave{\mathbf{w}}$ and off-diagonal matrix $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}$. The two parts are independent.
        - The diagonal vector $\grave{\mathbf{w}}$ is obtained by the Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA), which is used to obtain a weighted gradient not damage any tasks with optimization. MGDA can be easily solved by quadratic programming. The objective of MGDA is
        $$
        \grave{\mathbf{w}}^*= \arg\min\_{\mathbf{w}}\quad  \Big\Vert\sum\_i w\_i {g}\_i\Big\Vert^2,
            \text{s.t.}\quad \sum\_i \mathbf{w}\_i = 1\text{  and  }\mathbf{w}\_i\ge 0, \forall i .
        $$
        - The off-diagonal matrix $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}$: The objectives of any two rows in the $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}$ are different. For row $i$, the objective is the combination of non-diagonal entries, 
        $$
        \widetilde{\mathbf{W}}\_i^*=\mathop{\arg\min}\_\mathbf{w}\quad \left\\{\widehat{D}\left(\sum\nolimits\_{j\ne i}\mathbf{w}\_j{g}\_j,\mathbf{g}\_i\right)\Big|\forall i \in \mathcal{T}\right\\}.
        $$
- *How the authors design timelines and tasks?*: To address your concern, we illustrate the construction in the Appendix. In our experiments, we transform 3 image recognition datasets for PCL.
For effective transformation, several requirements are needed: (1) Random label set for each task, in which the data stream length of each task can be different; (2) Random timeline for each label set, in which the debut of each task can be any time between the first access of the former and latter tasks. For simplicity, we omit all blank time that all data streams are unavailable.
    - Parallel Split EMNIST (PS-EMNIST): We split EMNIST (62 classes) into 5 tasks and randomly generate 3 label sets for each task and 3 timelines for each label set (say 9 different situations). The size of the label set for each task, i.e., the number of classes, is set to larger than 2 while no more than 15.
    - Parallel Split CIFAR-100 (PS-CIFAR-100): We split CIFAR-100 into 20 tasks and randomly generate 3 label sets for each task and 3 timelines for each label set. The size of the label set for each task is set to larger than 2 while no more than 15.
    - Parallel Split ImageNet-TINY (PS-ImageNet-TINY): We split it into 20 tasks w.r.t. random 3 label sets, and each label set has 3 randomly generated timelines. The size of the label set for each task is set to larger than 5 while no more than 20.

> - (b) Here are some typos:

>   - (b6) Is D in Lemma 1 supposed to be non-negative or non-positive?

**A**: Thank you for your kind suggestion. We have corrected these typo errors in the revised manuscript (highlighted in cyan). Responses to (b4):
- We believe Eq. (1) and (3) are meaningful and necessary.
    - *The role of Eq. (1)(3)*: At any training step in PCL, multiple tasks make up a Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) problem. Eq. (1) reveals the dynamic MOO definition. At each optimization step, the goal of MOO is to optimize multiple objectives simultaneously while updating only once. In our paper, the only updated gradient is denoted as $\mathbf{d}^*$, and Eq (2) represents the update using $\mathbf{d}^*$. The question is how to obtain $\mathbf{d}^*$. The motivation of Eq. (3) is that for an objective in MOO, its own gradient $\mathbf{g}$ is the most qualified update direction. Thus, finding an optimal $\mathbf{d}^*$ with a small distance to $g$ becomes the new objective, i.e., $\min D(\mathbf{d}^*, \mathbf{g})$ in Eq (3). However, in MOO, we need to consider the distance from $\mathbf{d}^*$ to multiple objective-specific gradients, yielding the new MOO problem Eq (3).
    - We believe it is necessary to illustrate related preliminary before introducing the details of our proposed method.

content.title: Response to Reviewer KbKv (2)
content.comment:
> - How was Eq. (8) inferred? Some detail about Multiple Gradient Descent should be discussed before jumping to Eq. (8)

**A**: To address your concern, we have revised the manuscript to make the method clearer. 
- *Inferring of Eq (8)*: At the current time,
    - if $|\mathcal{T}|=1$, it means that we have only one task pass and there exists no training conflict. Thus, we use the task's own gradient to update, i.e., $\mathbf{d}^*=\mathbf{g}\_i$;
    - if $|\mathcal{T}|>1$, it means that we have at least two tasks and we need to solve the training conflict problem. In our work, we define to find the optimal weights $w^*$ and the final update gradient is obtained by $\mathbf{d}^*=\sum\_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbf{w}\_i\mathbf{g}\_i$. To avoid the self-interference problem, we use a matrix $W$ instead of the weight vector $w$, and solve it by using the proposed MaxDO approach. The weight matrix $W$ contains two parts, the diagonal vector $\grave{\mathbf{w}}$ and off-diagonal matrix $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}$. To satisfy the condition $\sum\_i \mathbf{w}^*\_i =1$: (1) For the diagonal $\grave{\mathbf{w}}$, we have $\sum\_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\grave{\mathbf{w}}\_i=1$ according to MGDA. (2) For the off-diagonal $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}$, we use softmax on each row, thus  $\sum\_{j\in\mathcal{T}}\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}\_{ij}=1$ for any row $i$. Thus, we have $\sum\_{i,j}{\mathbf{W}}\_{ij}=|\mathcal{T}|+1$. And in Eq (8), we divide the sum with $|\mathcal{T}|+1$ to guarantee the condition.

- *More details about MGDA*: We have added more description on MGDA in the revised manuscript. More details of MGDA can be seen in the Appendix.
    
    MGDA: 

    An elegant solution to the MOO for Pareto optimality[1] is the Steepest Descent Method (SDM)[2], which aims to obtain an optimal descent direction ${d}^*$ that satisfies
    $$
    \mathbf{d}^*,\alpha^* = \arg\min\_{\mathbf{d},\alpha} \quad \alpha+\frac{1}{2}\left\Vert \mathbf{d}\right\Vert^2,
    \text{s.t.}\quad \mathbf{g}\_i^\top \mathbf{d} \le \alpha,\quad\forall i \in \mathcal{T},
    $$
    where the constraints let each task have non-conflict with gradient ${d}$.
    Considering the Lagrange multipliers and Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) condition, the dual problem solved by the Multi-Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA)[3] is
    $$
    \mathbf{w}^*= \arg\min\_{{w}}\quad  \Big\Vert\sum\_i \mathbf{w}\_i \mathbf{g}\_i\Big\Vert^2,
        \text{s.t.}\quad \sum\_i \mathbf{w}\_i = 1\text{  and  }\mathbf{w}\_i\ge 0, \forall i .
    $$

    The objective of MGDA is $0$ and the resulting point satisfies the KKT conditions, or the solution gives a Pareto descent direction that improves all tasks.

- [1] Buchanan J M. The relevance of Pareto optimality. Journal of conflict resolution, 1962, 6(4): 341-354.
- [2] Jörg Fliege and Benar Fux Svaiter. Steepest descent methods for multicriteria optimization. Mathematical methods of operations research, 2000.
- [3] Jean-Antoine Désidéri. Multiple-gradient descent algorithm (mgda) for multiobjective optimization. Comptes Rendus Mathematique, 2012.



> - The authors should describe more details about the experiments in section 4. Are the results of previous MTL methods in Table 123 produced by yourself? The authors should provide more implementation details. The evaluation metrics and description of table 123 are also unclear.

**A**: To address your concern, we have shown more experiment details in the revised manuscript. 
- *More experimental details*: In our experiments, we take a 2-layer MLP as the backbone network for PS-EMNIST and a Resnet-18 for PS-CIFAR-100 and PS-ImageNet-Tiny. The learning rate is set to 0.003, 0.0004 and 0.0005 for PS-EMNIST, PS-CIFAR-100 and PS-ImageNet-Tiny. The SGD in MaxDO has a learning rate of 50. Each task is data stream, i.e., each data point passes only once. For each task, we set the batch size to 128 per step.
- *Method production*: Yes, since we are the first work studying PCL, all results of previous MTL methods are produced by ourselves with the claimed setting in their papers.
- *Evaluation metrics*: Following previous continual learning works, we leverage two metrics to evaluate PCL methods.
    - Final accuracy ($A\_T=\frac{1}{T} \sum\nolimits\_{t=1}^T a\_{\bar{e}}^t,$): This metric is evaluated on all seen tasks when the last task finishes its training.
    - Final Forgetting ($F\_T=\frac{1}{T} \sum\nolimits\_{t=1}^T a^t\_{\bar{e}}-a\_{e\_t}^t$):  This metric is the accuracy difference between the final accuracy and the accuracy when each task just finish their training.

> - I didn't find any explanation or analysis of Figure 2. How does figure 2 support this paper?

**A**: 
Please refer to the last paragraph in Sec. 3.2. In this paragraph, we compared our AGD metric with Euclidean and Cosine distances and showed why it is necessary to utilize our asymmetric distance in Problem (3).

content.title: Response to Reviewer KbKv (1)
content.comment:
Dear reviewer, we have revised the manuscript and reuploaded the revised version, where the contents in cyan are revised.

## Weaknesses: 
The paper contains some flaws in its presentation and analysis. I have the following questions.

> - The proposed artifact metric has a corollary shown in Eq.(5). The authors mention that when $\mathbf{g}\_A \ll \mathbf{g}\_b$, the metric has some tolerance 1/2. Is there some specific meaning for this 1/2 here? Why it has to be 1/2? The authors should provide more explanation about this. 

**A**: To explain the reason why we set a tolerance of $\frac{1}{2}$ in AGD, we take two parallel tasks A and B as an example at any time.
- When $\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}\\|\gg\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\\|$ and we update task B with $\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}$, the update produces huge impact on task B even if $\langle{\mathbf{g}}\_\text{A},\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\rangle>0$. This is because a much larger gradient may escape from a local minimum. Thus, we define that the distance $\widehat{D}({\mathbf{g}}\_\text{A},\mathbf{g}\_\text{B})$ in this situation should be large (near $1$).
- When $\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}\\|\ll\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\\|$, the update produces a mild impact on task B even if $\langle{\mathbf{g}}\_\text{A},\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\rangle<0$. That means that updating with a zero gradient will neither improve nor damage the performance. Even though, we prefer positive influence rather than non-influence. Thus, we define that the distance $\widehat{D}({\mathbf{g}}\_\text{A},\mathbf{g}\_\text{B})$ in this situation is the mid-level between the best ($\widehat{D}=0$) and worst ($\widehat{D}=1$).
- Note that the tolerance can be controlled by adding a factor $\gamma>0$. Omitting the edge situation, we have 
$$
\widehat{D}({\mathbf{g}}\_\text{A},\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}) = \frac{\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}-\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\\|}{\gamma \\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\\|+\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}-\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\\|}
$$
- The experiments on PS-CIFAR-100 with different tolerances are shown in the following table. The results show either larger or smaller tolerances compared to $\frac{1}{2}$ will get the performance drop. 

    |$\gamma$|Tolerance|$A\_T$|$F\_T$|
    |:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
    |0.2|$\frac{5}{6}$|69.283 |24.126 |
    |0.5|$\frac{2}{3}$|69.486  |24.520 |
    |1(ours)  |$\frac{1}{2}$|70.078  |24.907 |
    |2  |$\frac{1}{3}$|69.626 |24.344 |
    |3  |$\frac{1}{4}$|69.505 |24.479 |
    |4  |$\frac{1}{5}$|69.332  |24.600 |

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies parallel continual learning (PCL), a variant of continual learning in which tasks are processed asynchronously. That is, their availability during training is stochastic. Specifically, this paper tackles the problem of catastrophic forgetting and training conflict in PCL. Regarding catastrophic forgetting, the authors simply adopt existing methods that use replay-buffers. For the training conflict, the authors argue that they are produced by the interaction between task gradients during training, and propose a gradient-reweighting approach, MaxDO, which minimizes the maximum asymmetric discrepancy among multiply gradients. The proposed method is compared with MTL approaches in three different image recognition tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strenghts:**
- S1. The problem setting is interesting and understudied, and it provides a new environment where gradient conflict can occur.
- S2. The idea of having an asymmetric measure of discrepancy between gradients is really appealing and interesting.

**Weaknesses:**
- W1. While catastrophic forgetting is important in continual learning, I am not sure why does it have so much space in the experimental part, as the proposed approach is to use an existing solution.
- W2. The paper in general lacks intuition and justifications (more on that below).
- W3. Experimental results are marginally better.

Regarding W2: The manuscript have a number of assumptions and loose steps that need to be clarified:
- R1. Problem (1) and (3) are really loosely connected. What is the optimal d* supposed to be? And how does solving Eq. (3), which is tied to a specific local optimization process, connect with solving Eq. (1)?
- R2. What is the intuition behind the AGD metric? What does each of its argument represents semantically?
- R3. What does it mean to "have a tolerance of 1/2"? Why is that beneficial/desired?
- R4. Why is broadcasting the vector $w$ into a matrix $W$ justified? I guess it is to have independent parameters to solve Eq. (6), but why can we then combine them together?
- R5. Following R4, why can we combine these off-diagonal weights with MGDA? Even more, one of the steps is a local optimization process (SGD with Maximum Discrepancy), while the other is solved in one-step. Isn't there any harm in combing both approaches? And which learning rate do we set for the first step? is that important?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity and quality.** The manuscript would benefit a lot from some polishing. There are quite a few grammatically wrong phrases (e.g. "the min-distance problem should be asymmetry"), and phrases which I unfortunately do not understand (e.g. "symmetric metrics mean the forward and backward influences are treated as symmetric") or too convoluted (e.g. "the asymmetric metric does not require the symmetric property that D(x, y) = D(y, x) in symmetric metric.").

**Novelty.** The application and most of the proposed method is novel. Yet it should be emphasized that it relies in existing methods for catastrophic forgetting and on MGDA for gradient balancing.

**Literature review.**
- Continual Learning. While mostly complete, I feel the paper miss some works such as "[Orthogonal Gradient Descent for Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07104)" which orthogonalized gradients in continual learning to avoid catastrophic forgetting.
- Multitask Learning. The literature review regarding MTL leaves quite some room for improvement:
  - Relevant works such as [CAGrad](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14048), [RotoGrad](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.02631), and [GradVac](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.05874) were omitted.
  - To introduce MTL, conflicting gradients works are cited, instead of the seminal work by [Richard Caruana](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/A:1007379606734).
  - The statement "Most existing MTL methods formulate the problem into finding an optimal gradient" is completely wrong. Gradient conflict in MTL is a relative recent direction and there is extensive work on other directions such as clustering approaches and adaptive networks.
  - MGDA applied to the backbone parameters is not introduced by Sener & Koltum. Their contribution was to apply MGDA (by [Désidéri](https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1631073X12000738)) to the feature produced by the backbone.
  - Similarly, saying that any of the methods described in 4.3 are state-of-the-art is wrong. As of today, there is no a clear state-of-the-art method.

**Reproducibility.** The experiments are not reproducible, as important details such as the learning rate for Eq. (7) are not provided. The provided code only includes a single file with an implementation of the proposed method, which has been stripped down from the working code, as there are undeclared variables (e.g. variable `lr` in line 52).
content.summary_of_the_review: The application of conflicting gradient solutions to PCL is interesting and intriguing, and the paper contains nice ideas such as using asymmetric metrics to compute the conflict between gradients. However, results are only marginally better than existing approaches, writing needs to be improved, and there exist a number of flaws and unjustified steps which I consider needs to be revised and improved before acceptance.

content.title: Follow-up questions
content.comment:
Dear authors, I really appreciate the detailed response. While many of my questions were answered, and I see more clearly some of the intuitions you were trying to transmit, I still do have some follow-up questions after your reply:

1.  Which kind of dual problem is Eq. (6)? There are no contraints to be solved there, so it is clearly not a Lagrangian dual problem.
2. Provided the intuition of your metric: Why would you think that the worst case is $D(d^*, g) = 1$ instead of $D(-g, g) = \frac{2}{3}$? In the former case there is at least some exploration and randomness.
3. What I was trying to say in W2 R4 was that, even if you "decoupled" the parameters using a matrix $W$, this matrix is then collapsed into a vector $w$. Why should we expect $w_i = \sum_j w_{ij}$ to preserve any of the meaning for a _particular_ task? Don't we just shift the conflict to these weights instead? While you forced the problems to be solved independently, weights are combined and then dependent, given the observed weight values. Assume the case with two tasks: the matrixs will be 1 in the off-diagonal and assume the diagonal is really unbalanced (say, 0.95 vs. 0.05). Then the final weights will be 1.95 and 1.05 (or 0.65 and 0.35 if you forced them to the simplex). Why are these values semantically meaningful? Clearly the goal of MGDA is not achieved anymore. 
4. Re W2 R5:

content.comment:
Dear authors,

Your setup is not regular projected gradient descent. In PGD, you need to project back to the feasible set *each time you update your parameter*, but you are doing 5 steps of SGD with a high learning rate before projecting back. If your variation for solving the problem is equivalent to PGD and enjoys the same properties is not obvious to me and it should be discussed, as this directly affects your results.

Also, I just realized of something while looking closely at the optimization problem. Please let me know if I am wrong.

Assume you have a solution for the first part of the problem of Eq. 7 for a given i. Let me call that solution $w^*$ (openreview breaks with double sub-indices) and the followed direction $d^* = \sum_j w^*_j g_j$ with $j \neq i$. This means that $\hat{D}(d^*, g_i) \leq \hat{D}(d, g_i)$ for any other direction $d$ from the feasible set.
- Let me call $\epsilon^* = || d^* - g_i ||$, $\epsilon = || d - g_i|| $, and $C = ||g_i||$.
- Therefore $\hat{D}(d^*, g_i) \leq \hat{D}(d, g_i)$ is equal to $\frac{\epsilon^*}{C + \epsilon^*} \leq \frac{\epsilon}{C + \epsilon}$, which equals $\epsilon^*(C + \epsilon) \leq \epsilon(C + \epsilon^*)  \Leftrightarrow \epsilon^* C + \epsilon^* \epsilon \leq \epsilon C + \epsilon\epsilon^*  \Leftrightarrow \epsilon^* C \leq \epsilon C   \Leftrightarrow \epsilon^* \leq \epsilon$.
- This means that all the solutions of the proposed asymmetric distance equal the solutions of the problem $\min_d ||d - g_i|| $.

If my reasoning is right, I am not sure whether the proposed metric adds something new wrt existing symmetric metrics.

This is a standard projection operation, and the optimization is able to converge to a feasible solution as other iterative projection methods such as [1].

[1] Zhao Y B. Optimal k-thresholding algorithms for sparse optimization problems. SIAM Journal on Optimization, 2020, 30(1): 31-55.

> Assume you have a solution for the first part of the problem of Eq. 7 for a given i. Let me call that solution $w^\*$ (openreview breaks with double sub-indices) and the followed direction $d^\* = \sum\_j w^\*\_j g\_j$ with $j \neq i$. This means that $\hat{D}(d^\*, g\_i) \leq \hat{D}(d, g\_i)$ for any other direction $d$ from the feasible set.
> - Let me call $\epsilon^\* = || d^\* - g\_i ||$, $\epsilon = || d - g\_i|| $, and $C = ||g\_i||$.

> - This means that all the solutions of the proposed asymmetric distance equal the solutions of the problem $\min\_d ||d - g\_i|| $.

**A**:Thank you for your comment. Your deduction is correct only for one single gradient, but is not applicable for multiple gradients. We point out two mistakes in your deduction:

1.  > This means that $\hat{D}(d^\*, g\_i) \leq \hat{D}(d, g\_i)$ for any other direction $d$ from the feasible set.

    This statement is only correct for a single gradient with the single objective $\hat{D}(d, g\_i)$. In MOO, because of the conflict among objectives, a feasible solution to multiple objectives may be not the optimal solution to one of them. MOO seeks a whole improvement for multiple objectives simultaneously.

2. > This means that all the solutions of the proposed asymmetric distance equal the solutions of the problem $\min\_d ||d - g\_i|| $.

    Your deduction is only correct for one single gradient. We follow your notations and we have $n (n>1)$ gradients $\\{\mathbf{g}\_1,\cdots,\mathbf{g}\_n\\}$. We need to verify that $\sum\_i \hat{D}(\mathbf{d}^\*, \mathbf{g}\_i)\le\sum\_i \hat{D}(\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{g}\_i)$ instead of any of them such as $\hat{D}(\mathbf{d}^\*, \mathbf{g}\_i)\le\hat{D}(\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{g}\_i)$. We take $n=2$ for example and illustrate the difference.

    - Let $\epsilon\_1^\* = || \mathbf{d}^\* - \mathbf{g}\_1 ||$, $\epsilon\_1 = || \mathbf{d} - \mathbf{g}\_1|| $, $C\_1 = ||\mathbf{g}\_1||$ and $\epsilon\_2^\* = || \mathbf{d}^\* - \mathbf{g}\_2 ||$, $\epsilon\_2 = || \mathbf{d} - \mathbf{g}\_2|| $, $C\_2 = ||\mathbf{g}\_2||$.
    - If $\hat{D}(\mathbf{d}^\*, \mathbf{g}\_1)+\hat{D}(\mathbf{d}^\*, \mathbf{g}\_2)\le\hat{D}(\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{g}\_1)+\hat{D}(\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{g}\_2)$, then $\cfrac{\epsilon\_1^\*}{C\_1 + \epsilon\_1^\*}+\cfrac{\epsilon\_2^\*}{C\_2 + \epsilon\_2^\*}\le\cfrac{\epsilon\_1}{C\_1 + \epsilon\_1}+\cfrac{\epsilon\_2}{C\_2 + \epsilon\_2}$. 
        - Assume $\epsilon^\*\_1+\epsilon^\*\_2\le\epsilon\_1+\epsilon\_2$ and $C\_1=C\_2=C>0$.
        - $\Rightarrow (\epsilon^\*\_1+\epsilon^\*\_2)(\epsilon\_1\epsilon\_2-C^2)+2\epsilon\_1\epsilon\_2C \ge (\epsilon\_1+\epsilon\_2)(\epsilon\_1^\*\epsilon\_2^\*-C^2)+2\epsilon\_1^\*\epsilon\_2^\*C$
        - If $ \epsilon\_1\epsilon\_2\ge  C^2 $, then $(\epsilon\_1+\epsilon\_2)(\epsilon\_1\epsilon\_2-C^2)+2\epsilon\_1\epsilon\_2C \ge (\epsilon\_1+\epsilon\_2)(\epsilon\_1^\*\epsilon\_2^\*-C^2)+2\epsilon\_1^\*\epsilon\_2^\*C$,
        - Thus, we have $(\epsilon\_1\epsilon\_2-\epsilon\_1^\*\epsilon\_2^\*)(\epsilon\_1+\epsilon\_2+2C)\ge 0\Rightarrow \epsilon\_1\epsilon\_2\ge\epsilon\_1^\*\epsilon\_2^\*$.
        - In short, under the assumption, we have $\epsilon^\*\_1+\epsilon^\*\_2\le\epsilon\_1+\epsilon\_2\Rightarrow \epsilon\_1^\*\epsilon\_2^\*\le\epsilon\_1\epsilon\_2$.
        - The deduction of the above step is not always correct. For example, $\epsilon\_1^\* = 3, \epsilon\_2^\*=4, \epsilon\_1=2, \epsilon\_2=5$, we have $\epsilon\_1^\*\epsilon\_2^\*=12>\epsilon\_1\epsilon\_2=10$.

content.comment:
Dear reviewer, we answer your new questions as follows. We have also uploaded our source code in the supplementary material.

> 1. Which kind of dual problem is Eq. (6)? There are no contraints to be solved there, so it is clearly not a Lagrangian dual problem.

**A**: In fact, we misuse the word "dual", and we have removed the misleading word in the new version. What we want to present is we transform the problem with a large decision dimension into only searching in a probability simplex $\mathcal{W}=\\{\mathbf{w}:\sum\_i\mathbf{w}\_i=1 \text{  and  } \mathbf{w}\_i\ge 0\\}$. It is not practical to directly solve for $\mathcal{d}$ on each optimization step. 
This kind of method is named linear scalarization, which is the fastest variant for gradient-based learning, and it is a standard approach to solving MOO, e.g., [1][2][3]. 

- [1] Jean-Antoine Désidéri. Multiple-gradient descent algorithm (mgda) for multiobjective optimization. Comptes Rendus Mathematique, 2012.
- [2] Liu X, Tong X, Liu Q. Profiling pareto front with multi-objective stein variational gradient descent. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 2021, 34: 14721-14733.
- [3] Ruchte Michael, Josif Grabocka. Efficient multi-objective optimization for deep learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2103.13392 (2021).

> 2. Provided the intuition of your metric: Why would you think that the worst case is $D(d^\*, g) = 1$ instead of $D(-g, g) = \frac{2}{3}$? In the former case there is at least some exploration and randomness.

**A**: Our metric depends on not only the angle difference but also the magnitude difference between gradients. We hold the opinion that when the angle is 180°, $\mathbf{d}=-\mathbf{g}$ is not the worst case in $D(\mathbf{d},\mathbf{g})$. This is because $-\mathbf{g}$ may make the optimization still under control and $-100\mathbf{g}$ may directly fail the optimization, that is, the solution more quickly escapes from a local minimum.

> 3. What I was trying to say in W2 R4 was that, even if you "decoupled" the parameters using a matrix $W$, this matrix is then collapsed into a vector $w$. Why should we expect $w\_i = \sum\_j W\_{ij}$ to preserve any of the meaning for a particular task? Don't we just shift the conflict to these weights instead? While you forced the problems to be solved independently, weights are combined and then dependent, given the observed weight values. Assume the case with two tasks: the matrixs will be 1 in the off-diagonal and assume the diagonal is really unbalanced (say, 0.95 vs. 0.05). Then the final weights will be 1.95 and 1.05 (or 0.65 and 0.35 if you forced them to the simplex). Why are these values semantically meaningful? Clearly the goal of MGDA is not achieved anymore.


**A**:  
- We sum up each column of the weight matrix $\mathbf{W}$. And the goal is in two aspects:
    - For each off-diagonal entry of the first column, their sum means the effect of the gradient $\mathbf{g}\_1$ reducing the maximum discrepancy from other gradients.
    - In Eq. (7), we introduce the MGDA, which obtains a weighted gradient that does not damage any tasks with optimization. On one hand, MGDA is used to reduce the possible negative effect in only SGD. On the other hand, SGD (w/ Maximum discrepancy) reduces the training failure of new tasks in MGDA. Detailedly, in MGDA, the weights of small gradients are always LARGER than the weights of large gradients (See the MGDA's performance in Tables 1, 2 and 3). In this case, the new task may fail its training, which is not unacceptable in continual learning. In our experiment, we find that MGDA has some performance improvement based on reducing Maximum Discrepancy, but the improvement is limited, because the training processes of different tasks are different, which means gradients have large magnitude differences. In Eq. (7), SGD (w/ Maximum discrepancy) plays a leading role against MGDA, and MGDA plays only a supplementary role.
- When there are only two tasks, each task has only one other task and the first term of Eq. (7) is meaningless. Thus, in your two-task example $\mathbf{W}=\left[ \begin{matrix} 0.95&1 \\\\ 	1 & 0.05 \end{matrix}\right]\Rightarrow[1.95, 1.05]$, the off-diagonal entry $1$ is meaningless in reducing maximum gradient discrepancy but is useful to tackle the problem that the training of new task is restrained. We prefer to encourage new task training rather than meet Pareto optimality strictly. Note that, the two-task situation is not common in rehearsal-based PCL, because the rehearsal data stream also serves as an independent task.

> - W2 R3. What does it mean to "have a tolerance of 1/2"? Why is that beneficial/desired?

**A**: To explain the reason why we set a tolerance of $\frac{1}{2}$ in AGD, we take two parallel tasks A and B as an example at any time.
- When $\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}\\|\gg\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\\|$ and we update task B with $\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}$, the update produces huge impact on task B even if $\langle{\mathbf{g}}\_\text{A},\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\rangle>0$. This is because a much larger gradient may escape from a local minimum. Thus, we define that the distance $\widehat{D}({\mathbf{g}}\_\text{A},\mathbf{g}\_\text{B})$ in this situation should be large (near $1$).
- When $\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}\\|\ll\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\\|$, the update produces a mild impact on task B even if $\langle{\mathbf{g}}\_\text{A},\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\rangle<0$. That means that updating with a zero gradient will neither improve nor damage the performance. Even though, we prefer positive influence rather than non-influence. Thus, we define that the distance $\widehat{D}({\mathbf{g}}\_\text{A},\mathbf{g}\_\text{B})$ in this situation is the mid-level between the best ($\widehat{D}=0$) and worst ($\widehat{D}=1$).
- Note that the tolerance can be controlled by adding a factor $\gamma>0$. Omitting the edge situation, we have 
$$
\widehat{D}({\mathbf{g}}\_\text{A},\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}) = \frac{\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}-\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\\|}{\gamma \\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\\|+\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}-\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\\|}
$$
- The experiments on PS-CIFAR-100 with different tolerances are shown in the following table. The results show either larger or smaller tolerances compared to $\frac{1}{2}$ will get the performance drop. 

    |$\gamma$|Tolerance|$A\_T$|$F\_T$|

    |2  |$\frac{1}{3}$|69.626 |24.344 |
    |3  |$\frac{1}{4}$|69.505 |24.479 |
    |4  |$\frac{1}{5}$|69.332  |24.600 |

> - W2 R4. Why is broadcasting the vector $\mathbf{w}$ into a matrix $\mathbf{W}$ justified? I guess it is to have independent parameters to solve - Eq. (6), but why can we then combine them together?

**A**: The word "broadcast" means that we use a matrix $\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{T}|\times|\mathcal{T}|}$ instead a vector $\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{T}|}$. To make the illustration clearer, we delete the misleading word. Yes, the matrix $\mathbf{W}$ has each row optimized independently. 
- *Why use a matrix instead of a vector variables?*: Each objective of the dual problem (Eq. (6)) will be highly affected by the minimum discrepancy, i.e., each gradient itself. For example, by minimizing objective $\widehat{D}(\sum\nolimits\_j\mathbf{w}\_j\mathbf{g}\_j,\mathbf{g}\_i$), weight $\mathbf{w}\_i$ is more like to be activated than others. Thus, multiple objectives will be compromised by multiple self-interference but fail to reduce the maximum discrepancy in the dual problem optimization.
- *How to optimize with a matrix variable?*: The matrix can be decomposed into two parts. The diagonal vector is optimized via MGDA. The objectives of any two rows are different. 
    - The off-diagonal matrix $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}$: The objectives of any two rows in the $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}$ are different. For row $i$, the objective is the combination of non-diagonal entries, 
    $$
    \widetilde{W}\_i^*=\mathop{\arg\min}\_\mathbf{w}\quad \left\\{\widehat{D}\left(\sum\nolimits\_{j\ne i}\mathbf{w}\_j\mathbf{g}\_j,\mathbf{g}\_i\right)\Big|\forall i \in \mathcal{T}\right\\}.
    $$
    - The diagonal vector $\grave{{w}}$ is obtained by the Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm (MGDA), which is used to obtain a weighted gradient not damage any tasks with optimization. MGDA can be easily solved by quadratic programming. The objective of MGDA is
    $$
    \grave{{w}}^*= \arg\min\_{\mathbf{w}}\quad  \Big\Vert\sum\_i \mathbf{w}\_i \mathbf{g}\_i\Big\Vert^2,
        \text{s.t.}\quad \sum\_i \mathbf{w}\_i = 1\text{  and  }\mathbf{w}\_i\ge 0, \forall i .
    $$

content.comment:
> - W2. The paper in general lacks intuition and justifications (more on that below).
> Regarding W2: The manuscript have a number of assumptions and loose steps that need to be clarified:
> - W2 R1. Problem (1) and (3) are really loosely connected. What is the optimal d* supposed to be? And how does solving Eq. (3), which is tied to a specific local optimization process, connect with solving Eq. (1)? 

**A**: To address your concerns, we give more discussions and make them clearer.
- Eq. (1) is the classic Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) definition. At each optimization step, the goal of MOO is to optimize multiple objective functions simultaneously while updating only once.
- In our paper, the only updated gradient is denoted as $\mathbf{d}^*$, and Eq. (2) represents the update using $\mathbf{d}^*$. The subsequent question is how to obtain $\mathbf{d}^*$.
- The motivation of Eq. (3) is that for an objective function in MOO, its own gradient $\mathbf{g}$ is the most qualified update one (for both direction and magnitude). Thus, the optimal $\mathbf{d}^*$ should be with a small distance to $\mathbf{g}$, i.e., the new objective $\min D(\mathbf{d}^*, \mathbf{g})$ in Eq. (3). 
- However, in MOO, we need to consider the distance from $\mathbf{d}^*$ to multiple objective-specific gradients, yielding the new MOO problem Eq. (3).


> - W2 R2. What is the intuition behind the AGD metric? What does each of its argument represents semantically?

**A**: To address your concern, we have revised the description of AGD to make it clearer. 
- *Why do we propose AGD?*: As illustrated in the above answer, Eq. (3) denotes the new MOO problem to find an optimal $\mathbf{d}^*$ for the only update. The key question is how to define the distance in Eq. (3) to measure the gradient discrepancy. Popular choices of distances are symmetric, such as Euclidean distance. However, the model update is highly related to gradient magnitude and direction, which is asymmetric to model updating. Thus, we need to propose a feasible asymmetric distance in Eq (3).
- *Why is AGD designed in the form of Eq (4)?*: 
    - AGD considers both gradient directions and magnitude, which are the two key elements in the MOO problem. Directly optimizing with magnitude-aware distance values may lead to a solution close to large gradients. To mitigate the bias from the magnitude difference, we employ the magnitude ratio to represent the magnitude difference.
    - Considering the definition of asymmetric metric, we consider the edge situation when $\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}=\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}=\mathbf{0}$. The edge situation is almost unreachable in the optimization, which means that the solution is optimal for all conflict tasks.
- *The semantical meaning of the AGD features*: 
    - AGD is highly related to gradient directions and magnitude differences.
    - When $\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}\\|\gg\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\\|$, AGD has no tolerance and the distance is near 1, which means that a much larger gradient may destroy the learning of tasks with small gradients.
    - When $\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}\\|\ll\\|\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}\\|$, AGD has a tolerance $\frac{1}{2}$ even if $\langle{\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}},{\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}}\rangle<0$, which means the impact of ${\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}}$ on task B is small. Updating with a zero gradient will neither improve nor damage the performance.

> - W1. While catastrophic forgetting is important in continual learning, I am not sure why does it have so much space in the experimental part, as the proposed approach is to use an existing solution. 

**A**: Thanks for your suggestions. To address your concern, we explain the catastrophic forgetting as follows.
- To the best of our knowledge, we are the first work that studies the problem of Parallel Continual Learning (PCL). It is necessary to point out the two challenges of PCL including both training conflict and catastrophic forgetting. Moreover, the forgetting metric is important to continual learning, and our experimental results in this paper are provided as a benchmark for future PCL studies including solving catastrophic forgetting. 
- Different from traditional rehearsal, rehearsal memory is used to represent an independent task in PCL. Thus, the training conflict may worsen the forgetting of old tasks. That is, the new task produces large gradients and may mislead the replay of old tasks with small gradients. In our method, we consider reducing this gradient conflict and propose to measure the asymmetric gradient distance. Moreover, we propose to minimize the maximum discrepancy among multiple gradients. To show the effectiveness of MaxDO on rehearsal gradient, we evaluate the result that only leverages MaxDO on new tasks instead memory data stream (finished tasks). In this case, the final gradient is calculated by $\mathbf{d}=\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{g}\_\text{reherasal} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{g}\_\text{new}$, where $\mathbf{g}\_\text{new}$ is the solution gradient via MaxDO on only new tasks. The result shows that it is necessary to put the rehearsal gradient to the MaxDO. Otherwise, the model will get worse accuracy and weak forgetting.

## Weaknesses:

> 1. Since there are many different kinds of asymmetric distances, the paper should compare the proposed AGD with other asymmetric distances in analysis and experiments. 


**A**: Thank you for your suggestion. Following previous work [1][2][3][4], we design the two following asymmetric distance examples:

- Example distance 1 (ExDist1): $\alpha \in [0,1]$ is a random weight.

$$
D(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = \\|\mathbf{x}-\alpha \mathbf{y}\\|
$$

- Example distance 2 (ExDist2): $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are two random vectors $\mathbf{a}\_{i}\in[0,1], \mathbf{b}\_{i}\in[0,1]$.  

$$
D(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) =\\|\mathbf{a} \odot \mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b} \odot \mathbf{y} \\|
$$

|Metric|$A\_T$|$F\_T$|
|---|:---:|:---:|
|ExDist1|68.625|23.626|
|ExDist2|68.930|23.756|
|AGD    |70.078|24.907|

All the results show that the proposed AGD metric consistently outperforms all the other metrics. This is because the other asymmetric distances are not designed for gradient descent. In contrast, our AGD metric is built by considering both gradient angle and magnitude ratio, which is used to find an optimal descent direction that guarantees the new task training and old task keeping. 

- [1] Mennucci A C G. On asymmetric distances. Analysis and Geometry in Metric Spaces, 2013.
- [2] Chen Y C, Zheng W S, Lai J H, et al. An asymmetric distance model for cross-view feature mapping in person reidentification.TCSVT. 2016.
- [3] Dong W, Charikar M, Li K. Asymmetric distance estimation with sketches for similarity search in high-dimensional spaces. Proceedings of the annual international ACM SIGIR conference on Research and development in information retrieval. 2008.
- [4] Gordo A, Perronnin F, Gong Y, et al. Asymmetric distances for binary embeddings. TPAMI 2013.


> 2. It should give the details for optimizing the first term in Eq. (7) as AGD is nonsmooth. Moreover, it needs to check the coefficients in Eq.(8) satisfy the condition $\sum\_i \mathbf{w}\_i =1$ or give some explanations that why the choice of coefficients is necessary.

**A**: To address your concern, we have made the method clearer in the revised version.
- *Nonsmooth*: AGD is nonsmooth because we consider the edge situation when $\mathbf{g}\_\text{A}=\mathbf{g}\_\text{B}=\mathbf{0}$ to meet the definition of asymmetric metric in Lemma 1. The edge situation is almost unreachable in neural network optimization. Even though, the edge situations in Eq. (4) have no effects on the training of the problem in Eq. (7). This is similar to the L1 norm in many neural networks, such as [1][2]. When all gradients are zero, we set the final weights to $\cfrac{1}{n}$, i.e, average weights.
- *Training details of the first-term in Eq. (7)*: $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}$, optimized by Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), is used to make up the maximum gradient discrepancy for each row. The objectives of any two rows in $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}$ are different and independent. For row $i$, to formulate the maximum discrepancy of gradient $\mathbf{g}\_i$, the objective is the combination of non-diagonal entries. The weighted other gradients should be with the smallest asymmetric distance to $\mathbf{g}\_i$.
- *Condition $\sum\_i \mathbf{w}\_i =1$*: Yes, our solution satisfies the condition $\sum\_i \mathbf{w}^*\_i =1$. The weight matrix $W$ contains two parts, the diagonal vector $\grave{\mathbf{w}}$ and off-diagonal matrix $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}$. The two parts are independent. Therefore,
    - For the diagonal vector $\grave{{w}}$, we have $\sum\_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\grave{\mathbf{w}}\_i=1$ according to MGDA.
    - For the off-diagona $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}$, we use softmax on each row, thus  $\sum\_{j\in\mathcal{T}}\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}\_{ij}=1$ for any row $i$.
    - To sum up, we have $\sum\_{i,j}{\mathbf{W}}\_{ij}=|\mathcal{T}|+1$. And in Eq (8), we divide the sum with $|\mathcal{T}|+1$ to guarantee the condition.
- *Necessity of the coefficients*: To show the necessity of the choice of coefficients, we evaluate the naive equal coefficients, and each value is set to $\cfrac{1}{n}$, that is, the results are the average of gradients. The compared results of the average weight methods and the proposed MaxDO method are shown as follows. It is clear that a good choice of coefficients is important to the control of the target gradient. 

    |Coefficients|$A\_T$|$F\_T$|
    |---|:---:|:---:|
    |average (1/n)  |68.682|24.645|
    |AGD            |70.078|24.907|

- [2] Wen W, Wu C, Wang Y, et al. Learning structured sparsity in deep neural networks. In NeurIPS, 2016.

content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn: This paper proposes a novel approach to an understudied training setting, parallel continual learning, in which heterogeneous tasks are continually streamed during training. The paper proposes an approach for how to construct a weight update combining the gradients from different tasks. To this end, the authors introduce an asymmetric distance metric and attempt to find a weight update jointly minimizing the distance between the update and the task gradients with respect to this metric. They compare this approach against various PCL baselines. Unfortunately, the reviewers found shortcomings with the work and presentation. At a high level, the reviewers did not find the particular choice of asymmetric distance metric well motivated, and were not convinced by the performance gains. At a more detailed level, reviewer 6yMu was not clear that the approach used to find an approximate solution to the constrained optimization problem yielding the weight update rule was well structured, and their concerns weren’t sufficiently addressed.
